questions.stem: Over a client's back, the nurse hears crackles and notes dullness on the lower left side, below the shoulder blade. Which lobe is most likely affected?
options: The left upper lobe
The right lower lobe
The lingula of the left upper lobe
The left lower lobe
questions.rationale:
The left lower lobe fills most of the lower back on the left, so findings low on the left side of the back come from it.

The lingula isn't the right answer: it's the lower part of the left upper lobe, but it lies at the front of the chest, so it's heard from the front. The right lower lobe is on the other side.

Takeaway: The lower lobes fill most of the back; the lingula and the right middle lobe are heard from the front.

questions.stem: After a neck injury at the level of C3 to C5, a client's breathing becomes weak and shallow. Which muscle's nerve supply was most likely affected?
options: The intercostal muscles, through the thoracic nerves
The sternocleidomastoid, through the accessory nerve
The diaphragm, through the phrenic nerve
The abdominal muscles, through the lumbar nerves
questions.rationale:
The phrenic nerve comes from the C3 to C5 levels of the spinal cord and controls the diaphragm, the main muscle of breathing in. An injury at that level can weaken it, so breathing becomes weak and shallow.

The intercostal muscles aren't the right answer: they help lift the ribs, but their nerves leave the spinal cord in the chest, below the injury. The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory muscle, and the abdominal muscles work mainly in forceful breathing out.

Takeaway: C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive: the phrenic nerve runs the main breathing muscle.

questions.stem: A nurse is auscultating a client's right lung. For each place where crackles are heard, click to specify the lobe they most likely come from.
rows: Just below the right collarbone, at the front
At the front, between the 4th and 6th ribs
Over the lower right back
Over the top of the right shoulder blade, on the back
Over the right side of the back, near the bottom of the ribs
questions.rationale:
The right upper lobe lies above the horizontal fissure: under the collarbone at the front, and over the top of the back. The right middle lobe lies between the horizontal and oblique fissures, at the front, between the 4th and 6th ribs. The right lower lobe fills most of the back below the shoulder blade.

Putting the lower back with the middle lobe is a mistake: the middle lobe lies at the front, and almost all of the back below the shoulder blades is lower lobe.

Takeaway: Front: upper and middle lobes. Back: mostly lower lobes, with the upper lobes at the top.

questions.stem: Place the structures that lymph from the leg passes through on its way back to the blood, in order.
items: A vein at the base of the neck
questions.rationale:
Lymph starts as tissue fluid taken up by lymphatic capillaries, moves through lymph vessels whose valves keep it flowing one way, and is filtered in the inguinal nodes in the groin. It then collects in the cisterna chyli, rises in the thoracic duct, and empties into a vein at the base of the neck.

Putting the nodes after the thoracic duct is a mistake: lymph is filtered in the nodes along the way, before it reaches the large ducts.

Takeaway: Capillaries → vessels → nodes → cisterna chyli → thoracic duct → vein.

questions.stem: Months after lymph nodes were removed from a client's left armpit during breast cancer surgery, her left arm is swollen. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The lymph from your arm has fewer nodes and vessels to drain through, so fluid builds up.”
“The nodes that remain have an infection from the surgery, which is making your arm swell.”
“Without those lymph nodes, your arm makes extra fluid to fight off infection.”
“The surgery weakened the arteries in your arm, which now leak blood into the tissue.”
questions.rationale:
The axillary nodes and their vessels drain the arm and breast. With them removed, the arm's lymph has fewer routes back to the blood, so fluid collects in the tissue: lymphedema.

The infection choice isn't the right answer: a swollen arm is more prone to infection, but swelling that came on months later, without fever or redness, comes from the lost drainage. The arm doesn't make extra fluid, and the arteries weren't removed.

Takeaway: Axillary nodes removed → arm lymphedema, from lost drainage.

questions.stem: A client with an infected ingrown toenail on the right big toe has tender, enlarged lymph nodes. Where should the nurse expect to find them?
options: In the left groin
In the right armpit
Behind the right ear
In the right groin
questions.rationale:
Lymph from the foot and leg drains to the inguinal nodes in the groin on the same side: the right groin.

The left groin isn't the right answer: lymph drains to the nodes on the same side as the infection. The armpit nodes drain the arm and chest, and the nodes behind the ear drain the scalp.

Takeaway: Foot and leg: inguinal nodes, on the same side.

questions.stem: A client has an abscessed tooth on the right side of the lower jaw. Which finding should the nurse expect when palpating the lymph nodes?
options: Tender, enlarged nodes on the left side of the neck
Tender, enlarged nodes on the right side of the neck
Tender, enlarged nodes in the right armpit
Hard, painless nodes on the right side of the neck
questions.rationale:
Infections of the mouth, teeth, and throat drain to the cervical nodes on the same side, which become tender and enlarged as their lymphocytes respond.

Hard, painless nodes isn't the right answer: they're on the right side, but nodes reacting to an infection are tender; hard, painless, fixed nodes need follow-up for other causes. The left side and the armpit don't drain the right jaw.

Takeaway: Head and neck infections: tender cervical nodes on the same side.
